speechtext:

2.	The following areas and localities have been designated: National employment service local office areas-Amherst, N.S., New Glasgow, N.S., Springhill, N.S., Newcastle, N.B., Drummondville, P.Q., Cornwall, Ontario, Elliot Lake, Ontario, Windsor, Ontario; Localities- Louisburg, N.S., Grand Falls-St. Leonard, N.B., Milltown, N.B., Port Elgin, N.B., Sack-ville, N.B., Campbellton, N.B., Louisville, P.Q., Matane, P.Q., Tracy, P.Q., La Broquerie, Manitoba, Drumheller, Alberta.

4.	The employment effects of the capital cost allowance program have been twofold. In many cases, immediate employment has been given to construction workers in the erection of new or expanded premises. Industries supplying materials, equipment and machinery have also benefited. In many cases, the new plants will not be completed for several months and the full employmentgiving impact of these new industries may
not be fully realized for some months. In total, we believe that a large number of workers will find jobs in surplus manpower areas because of the program.
5.	To date a total of 66 new industries have been established under the program. These industries will be producing close to 100 new products. In addition, the department is examining a considerable number of other applications and these will result in the establishment of more facilities to produce new products.
6.	Because many of these industries are in the process of being established, that is, having plants erected, buying machinery, etc., it is not possible to know how many workers they will ultimately employ. At the present time, they are giving employment to substantial numbers of construction workers who are erecting new and expanded plants. Furthermore, employment in machinery and equipment supplying industries has been assisted through the orders placed by these new industries. subtopic: INCREASE IN INFECTIOUS HEPATITIS
INCREASE IN INFECTIOUS HEPATITIS
speechtext:
Is the Minister of National Health and Welfare in a position to explain the increase in the incidence of infectious hepatitis in Canada in the past year?
Answer by: Mr. Monteith (Perth):
The reason for the increased incidence of infectious hepatitis in Canada last year is not known precisely. However probably the reasons are (1) the tendency for the disease to appear in cycles and (2) better reporting of the disease.
Infectious hepatitis is most common in children and young adults. Many infections are mild, develop no jaundice, and are recognizable only by liver function tests. The mode of spread of infectious hepatitis is similar to that of intestinal infections. The principal mode of spread of this disease is probably through intimate person to person contact.

subtopic: BLIND PERSONS ALLOWANCE
BLIND PERSONS ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
1.	Has the government received representations from any organizations, requesting a specific allowance for blind persons of $25 a month free of a means test, to compensate for extra expenses incurred because of blindness?
2.	If so, from what organizations have such representations been received, and what answer has the government made?
Answer by: Mr. Monteith (Perth):
1.	Yes.
2.	Representations were made by a joint deputation of the Canadian Council of the Blind and the Canadian National Institute for the Blind on September 26 last. The Minister of National Health and Welfare in meeting with this group indicated the desire on the part of the government to be helpful to blind persons and that their representations would receive very careful consideration. He mentioned that in any steps taken to improve Canada's social welfare legislation the needs of blind persons would certainly be included and that in this regard it was hoped that further steps would be taken at the next session of parliament.
A number of these steps have already been announced. The increase in the maximum benefit to $65 a month and the provision of a higher income ceiling under the Blind Persons Act will with the co-operation of the provinces bring added income to more than 8,500 blind persons across Canada. The increase in the federal old age security pension to $65 a month will bring higher benefits to between 10,000 and 11,000 blind persons now covered by that program. The proposal for the establishment of a national council of welfare at this time is for the purpose of advising on the federal government's social assistance programs including the Blind Persons Act; the representations made by organizations representing blind persons with respect to the further improvement of legislation affecting the blind are of course especially important in the consideration of this question. The fourth step relates to plans, if the provinces agree to a constitutional amendment, to introduce an old age survivors and disability insurance program which would include social insurance protection against blindness along with other disabilities.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. I wonder whether the minister is yet in a position to report, as a result of his discussions, with regard to the lay-offs of employees of the Cockshutt Farm Equipment Limited plant in Brantford. subtopic: BRANTFORD, ONT.    DISMISSAL OF EMPLOYEES OF IMPLEMENT COMPANY
speechtext:
Mk. Speaker, the hon. member for Assiniboia is following up the question he posed to me yesterday. Since then I have had a long discussion with the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Wratten) who is vitally interested in this matter, and I have contacted the national employment service office in Brantford.
We have received a report from the Brantford national employment service office that a part of the Cockshutt Farm Equipment plant is in process of sale to the White Motor Company and its affiliate the Oliver Farm Equipment Company. It is understood that this sale has been approved by the directors of Cockshutt Farm Equipment Limited and recommended to the shareholders.
Lay-offs have occurred at the plant over the last three weeks while some employees, it is understood, have left of their own accord to accept other employment. The Brantford national employment service office is finding employment within commuting distance of Brantford for some skilled tradesmen, while others are finding employment through personal contacts with other employers. One employer from outside the Brantford area has interviewed skilled tradesmen with a view to their employment elsewhere.
The prospect of alternative employment for the semi-skilled and unskilled workers is less bright at this moment. However, the situation concerning all those laid off is still somewhat uncertain until the sale has been completed and the intention of the new owners concerning the operation of the plant has become known. The national employment service office is keeping in close contact with the situation and will do everything possible to re-establish as quickly as possible the men who are being and will be laid off.
As to severance pay, that is not a matter which comes within federal jurisdiction. The agricultural implement industry is under provincial jurisdiction.

613. Special services branch including the promotion of a program for combating seasonal unemployment, the organization and use of workers for farming and related industries and assistance to the provinces under agreements entered into with the provinces by the Minister of Labour with the approval of the governor in council-further amount required, $90,000.

Mr. Chairman, this item in the further supplementary estimates for $90,000 is an amount required in connection with our do it now campaign. There has not been a complete statement on the functions of this campaign and the goal that we have in mind, or the participation that is involved in this campaign along with the promotional work undertaken by the federal government. Today I will try to give the members of the committee as full and complete a report on this item as is available.
This money is to provide for additional publicity material in the way of posters, pamphlets and advertising to support the efforts of and fulfil requests from our winter employment committees in towns and cities from coast to coast. This national campaign is designed to encourage individuals, businesses, industries and householders to carry out as much work as possible during the cold months. This program has reached a degree of effectiveness in the last couple of years which has resulted in positive effects on business activity in a wide variety of areas each year, and particularly each winter.
While there is still much to be done, the construction and supply industries have proven beyond any doubt, Mr. Chairman, that construction of all types can be a year round activity. The Canadian Construction Association reported in a bulletin dated November 30, 1961, as follows:
During the past eight years, increased efforts have been made by government at all levels, by individuals, by communities and by national organizations to stimulate winter employment. These have met with a substantial measure of success. As a matter of fact, the volume of wintertime construction and employment has increased so that now more Canadians are employed in construction operations in mid-winter than were employed during the so-called building season a dozen years ago.
This is the end of the quotation that appeared in this bulletin issued by the Canadian Construction Association on November 30 last. In further support of this statement I should like to quote from the September, 1961 issue of the National Builder, a magazine which is closely associated with the National House Builders Association. I quote:
The swing to year round operation in building has made faster headway among the general contractors, but now it seems that home builders are catching up fast, encouraged by the easy availability of mortgage loans, the increasing

Supply-Labour
number of pre-sold houses, and the advantages of getting their latest designs on the market for the growing spring market.
Recently the editor of this magazine sent us the following message relating this trend to our do it now campaign. His message read thus:
You will be interested to know the do it now winter work campaign is converting the building industry across Canada to a stabilized year round operation from former spring to fall activities. Winter home building particularly now goes ahead in volume for a newly created winter-spring sales market.
That is the end of his remarks. Another authoritative magazine, the Building Supply Dealer-I might say at this time, Mr. Chairman, this magazine has vigorously supported the do it now campaign and its principle over the past several years-reports an increasing winter business amongst lumber dealers during each of the past few winters. In the December issue of Lumber Merchandising, another trade paper which serves the construction industry, the editor stated as follows, referring to the do it now campaign:
The idea of having work done in the winter months has been promoted consistently for the past few years and every year the accumulated effort helps produce more results for the current season.
Now, Mr. Chairman, during the past winter, from November to March, government sponsored N.H.A. home improvement loans increased over the previous year by 63 per cent and in total dollar value by 115 per cent, reaching almost $16 million. Government backed farm improvement loans increased by 51 per cent and the dollar value by 53 per cent, reaching a total of some $3.5 million.

Will my hon. friend permit me to make an observation? In view of the related nature of the item now before us and the more important one of $40 million, may we not consider both these items at the same time? The minister is now making a speech that would apply in part at any rate to both these items, and so for convenience of discussion, we would all be in order if we might consider both items together if this is agreeable.

speechtext: The unanimous consent of the committee would be required, of course.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the discussion has been exhausted, both items will carry.
Agreed.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. This means that during the winter months almost $19 million more was spent than in the winter previous on home and farm improvements. We hope for similar results this year. One large lending agency specializing in the building supply field reported an increase of 400 per cent in last winter's business over the previous winter, and attributed it largely to the effects of the do it now winter works campaign. They have just reported that during this past December their home improvement loan business equalled their entire winter business of last year, indicating, I submit, a marked increase this year over last year.
Further support of marked increases in winter construction activity is found in reports from 1600 lumber dealers, painting and decorating contractors and plumbers who tied their business promotions in with the do it now campaign we sponsored. The building supply dealers reported an average increase in their sales last winter of 19 per cent as a result of their participation in this campaign. Painting and decorating contractors reported a 21 per cent increase in their business, while plumbing and heating contractors had a 10 per cent increase.
In view of the heavy publicity campaign and advertising being carried out through all media at the present time, I should like to point out that more than 90 per cent of all we see and hear promoting the do it now principle is either contributed as a public service or paid for by business and industry, and this is all done as a result of the promotion that has been carried out in regard to the winter works do it now campaign. We estimate that we receive at least $10 public service support for every dollar we spend on behalf of the do it now campaign, and public support will again exceed $3 million this winter.
I take this opportunity of paying tribute to the hundreds of public spirited business enterprises, as well as to the newspapers, magazines, radio stations, television stations, public spirited companies and others that are so generous in supporting this national campaign. In addition to the paid public service support, it is very encouraging to me, and I am sure to all of us, to note that the direct advertising, whether in news or services by business and industry, has been increasing each winter, resulting in a reversal of old habits and customs of waiting for spring. On the radio last winter there were 37,000 spot

announcements, either sponsored or contributed as a public service by 220 radio stations, as well as 400 hours of program time discussing the do it now campaign. Television stations carried almost 80,000 spot announcements, either contributed by themselves, their advertisers or the C.B.C.
Advertising tied in with the do it now theme in newspapers has produced a total sum of 1,500 pages, and in addition newspapers carried more than 4,200 news stories. The poster advertising association of Canada and its member companies contributed 2,000 billboards as a public service across Canada, and thousands of merchants placed our poster material in their shop windows.
Excellent leadership has been provided at the local level by the national employment service and by some 195 winter employment campaign committees in all parts of Canada. The local campaigns which they developed have enlisted the full support of municipal governments, boards of trade, labour unions, women's groups, service clubs, banks, contractors, retail merchants, public utilities, churches and a variety of community groups. I also want to place on record my sincere appreciation of the efforts and support forthcoming from hundreds of private citizens who have helped to organize effective local campaigns in co-operation with the local employment offices.
Doing our best to practice what we preach, all departments within the federal government which are in a position to contribute to winter employment are doing so on an increasing scale. The departments which carry out construction and maintenance projects have set a good example in planning their operations so that a maximum amount of work will be carried out during the winter months.
The value of repair, alteration and maintenance work scheduled for the winter has averaged more than $10 million for the past four years, and will exceed this figure during the present winter. Procurement has also been specifically initiated or rescheduled in order to provide maximum winter work. The provincial governments have also taken effective steps to increase their construction, maintenance and procurement activities during the winter months.
There is not much else I can add to my statement on this particular item, and since the committee has agreed that we should consider both items at the same time I shall now give some idea of what is entailed in the next item of $40 million, known to all of us as the municipal winter works incentive program.
As in previous winters, these payments cover one half the payroll costs on accepted
Supply-Labour
projects from October 15, 1961 to a date to be determined by order in council. This is exactly the same as it was last year. In previous years the closing date was set at April 30 in the first supplemental vote, and this date was extended to May 31 in subsequent supplemental votes. Last year the vote was changed to provide for flexibility, if required at April 30 or close to that date.
The program was first introduced in 1958 as a part of the government's over-all action to create additional winter employment and, through performance, has proven most successful. It is now in its fourth winter and has provided an increased number of jobs each year. These have been mainly in the construction industry, where traditionally in Canada unemployment during the winter months has been high.
During the first winter, 1958-59, the number of men hired for on-site work was estimated at 41,500. That was when the opposition described the program as "peanuts" and "a bagatelle". During the second winter, 1959-60, the number of men hired was 51,600, and this was again described by the opposition in the same terms.
In relation to the total problem.

Last winter the number was
121,000	and already this winter the figure has reached 111,200. I might point out, as I have done in the past, that at least as many more persons have received employment or guarantees of employment each winter on off-site work, in the supply of materials used in the various projects.
The program was introduced as something of an experiment in 1958 to help stimulate work during the winter months, and the results achieved prove that it is a most useful method of attacking seasonal unemployment. Proof of that statement is the fact that the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, among others, supported the program from the outset as being a desirable means of providing additional winter employment and, at the same time, enabling municipalities to undertake much needed public services.
However, there were some who felt the program had little chance of success and that it would not appeal to the local governments. Now, to refute that, the increased number of municipalities that have taken advantage of the program each winter clearly indicates that it does appeal to municipalities; and the amount of work undertaken, together with the number of jobs created, are evidence that the program is effectively fulfilling its purpose.

Supply-Labour
During the first two winters, as an example, the program applied to certain specified categories of projects such as the construction and major improvement of roads, streets and sidewalks, the construction and major improvement of water, sewage and drainage facilities and the construction and development of municipal parks and playgrounds. These categories were then extended under last winter's program to include construction, major reconstruction or renovation of municipal buildings. The program for the current winter has again been broadened to cover any capital undertaking of a municipality, with only a few exceptions. The major exceptions are work on schools and hospitals. The reason for this is that the federal government participates in these fields and grants assistance under other measures.
The present program covers all the categories of projects which qualified in previous years, as well as many additional classes of projects. This year's program has been further broadened to include projects carried out in unorganized settlements, provided the work is sponsored by a community organization and carried out under acceptable community and provincial supervision. The current program also provides for participation by Indian bands, as was the case last winter and the winter before.
Up to the present time this year we have received 6,121 applications under this program, of which 6,048 have been accepted. Of the remainder, some have been rejected and some are pending decision.
How many have been accepted?
The number accepted is 6,048.
And 6,121 have come in?

Yes. Some are pending decision. The estimated total cost of those applications which have been accepted to date is $257J million. Of this amount it is estimated that $200 million will be expended during the period of the program, which commenced on October 15, 1961. The estimated total payroll costs of the projects which have been accepted during the period of the program is $66 million and the estimated federal government share is, of course, $33 million, 50 per cent of the payroll costs.
It is estimated that these undertakings which have been approved to date will provide employment for 111,200 men, for a total of 4,743,000 man days of work. Last winter's program did not reach these proportions until mid-April.
A total of 647 municipalities participated in the program during the winter of 1958-59.

That was the first winter in which this program was put into effect. The following year, during the winter of 1959-60 a total of 869 municipalities and Indian bands undertook projects under the program. Therefore there was an increase of over 200 municipalities participating during the second winter of the program.
With the broadening of the program last winter a total of 2,163 municipalities and Indian bands participated. That was three times as many as the winter before. Under this winter's program a total of 2,286 municipalities, Indian bands and unorganized settlements have submitted projects to date. This is an increase over last year of 120 municipalities so far this winter which are participating.
Some provinces, in co-operating with us in order to help in this situation, are granting additional assistance to the municipalities by making a financial contribution toward the payroll costs of projects approved under the program.
Six provinces?
I was just coming to that.
I just ask the question.
How many, did you say?
Six, is it not?

It is seven. I should like to list the provinces which are participating in this form of contribution and give their contributions. Prince Edward Island contributes 25 per cent; Quebec contributes 40 per cent; Ontario contributes 25 per cent; Manitoba contributes 25 per cent in respect of persons who are not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits, and 50 per cent in respect of persons who have been in receipt of social welfare assistance for a specified period. Saskatchewan contributes 25 per cent; Alberta contributes 25 per cent; British Columbia contributes 25 per cent plus an additional 25 per cent in respect of persons who have been in receipt of social welfare assistance for a specified period.
Under the laws of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia these provinces carried out work in rural municipalities that is of a nature normally considered to be a municipal function. Projects of this nature are acceptable under the municipal winter works incentive program, and in these instances the provinces contribute 50 per cent of the payroll costs of approved projects and bear the costs of materials and services.
I indicated earlier that in addition to creating jobs the municipal winter works incentive program has been of benefit to municipalities

in enabling them to provide much needed public services. In this connection I should like to point out that the program since its inception has contributed to the construction and major improvement of roads, streets and sidewalks having a total value of $167 million; to the construction and improvement of water, sewage and drainage facilities totalling $481 million and parks and playground facilities worth $36 million, while $78 million has been spent on the construction, major reconstruction or renovation of municipal buildings. This represents in all a total of more than $762 million in municipal works since the program began. This is a truly worthwhile program, Mr. Chairman.
Applications covering projects under the program are being received daily. There is an almost hourly change in the program. In my opinion there is no doubt at all that the number of municipalities participating and the volume of work provided this winter will be considerably larger than under last winter's program. We are endeavouring, with success, to interest more and more municipalities to participate in this program. Once they have entered it they want more of it. They are continually participating and being joined by other municipalities. In view of the excellence of this program I am sure the committee will find no difficulty in passing these estimates.

In the light of the fact that as of the last reported period there were 413,000 Canadians out of work, and bearing in mind that this was in the month of December, a period when the seasonal rise normally begins to take on a more acute form in our pattern of unemployment, not too much satisfaction can be derived from the statement made by the minister.
The hon. gentleman says that the do it now campaign for which he is asking a vote of $90,000 is carried out largely by business promotion and promotions generally under the auspices of non-government bodies. Likewise, one has to draw the conclusion from the circumstances surrounding federal participation in the winter works program that the bulk of this program is not carried on by the federal government but by the municipalities and the provinces. Notwithstanding this, the government gives the impression that through this program, of which it seeks to claim authorship, it is embarking on a vigorous measure to correct unemployment.
The fact is that this program, as it is, is not good enough. The fact is that this program neither at the present time nor since it came into being has dealt with the problem of unemployment which faces us in this country. There were 413,000 people out of work in the month of December. We do not
Supply-Labour
know what the figure is as of this date, January 31, 1962. Normally we would have received that figure some time around the 20th of the month, and perhaps before this debate is over the minister might explain why we have not received it as yet. In any event, this program cannot be regarded as satisfying the needs of Canada with regard to unemployment at this time.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Is he asking about the bureau of statistics figures on employment and unemployment for December?

No; for the last
reported period. We should have had them on January 20.
On January 20 the hon. member received them for December, and he will not receive the January figures until the middle of February.
I know, but the minister could easily have given us an interim report.
Give your own figures.

I am asked to give my own. Well, I will tell the committee this, and it is something everyone in this country knows. The problem of unemployment in Canada continues to be the major domestic problem facing us, and this government cannot, by a program of this kind, satisfy the Canadian people that it is resolutely and adequately confronting the problem. We welcome any measure taken to mitigate these fluctuations of employment, particularly those due to seasonal causes; but we are acutely aware, as I am sure the country is aware, that solutions of the type now being put forward do not go to the root of the unemployment problem.
It is, of course, characteristic of seasonal unemployment that it is most likely to occur in those very regions which suffer most from chronic unemployment. I have in mind, for example, the Atlantic provinces where unemployment since 1957 has been running at nearly twice the level of unemployment in the country as a whole. The seasonal swing in those provinces is twice as large as it is in Canada as a whole.
This government has not met the problem of unemployment. It certainly is not confronting the question as the President of the United States is. When one examines President Kennedy's state of the union message and the statement he made one week later, and compares the comprehensive measures envisaged by the government of the United States with the haphazard, laissez faire manner in which this government is meeting the problem, even a few months, or a short time

Supply-Labour
before a general election, one will not find it difficult to justify the condemnation which again we level at this government at this time for the way it is handling the problem of unemployment. There can be no doubt that the government has not yet given us any evidence of a program designed to carefully, thoroughly and effectively meet this problem. We say this program is satisfactory as far as it goes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? The hon. gentleman referred to the proposals advanced by the President of the United States. Would the hon. member indicate any suggestions made by President Kennedy that were not already introduced by this government some time ago?

I shall certainly do so before I complete my remarks, Mr. Chairman. The Prime Minister and other hon. gentlemen opposite make continued reference to the fact that the government of the United States is following the government of Canada in its handling of this problem. The Prime Minister, however, is unable to back up that rhetorical observation. The fact is that the government of the United States has confronted this problem vigorously and has given an example to this government. This government's big answer to those who suggest that the problem has not been adequately met is to refer to the winter works program.
They are just going to consider this program in the United States.

The Minister of Labour says that this program has to date provided employment for 111,000 people representing approximately 4 million man days of work. What does that mean? Let us find out from the minister what that statement really means when shorn of its verbiage and extravagance. How many men out of the 413,000 unemployed, according to recent figures-disregarding what the figure is as of this date- have been put to work for more than one week? How many men have been given work lasting throughout the period of the winter season? It is all very well to say that a certain number of men were put to work-
I am able to answer that question now if the hon. member wishes.
The minister may speak when I have finished.

The hon. gentleman asked a question and I am prepared to answer. If the hon. member will divide 111,000 persons into
4,700,000	days of work he will find it averages out to 45 days per man.
There we have the answer, Mr. Chairman; 45 days per man. This government says it has solved this problem by providing 45 man days of employment to 111,000 people.
Nine weeks' work.

Do we require a better illustration of the inadequacy of this program than the reply just given by the Minister of Labour? Last year almost 12 per cent of our work force was unemployed-*
715,000	people-and less than 200,000 people were put to work for limited periods only under this program; yet the government says that the winter works program must be regarded as having satisfactorily solved the problem.
Let us examine the real facts. Last year the minister said the program cost $200 million. He said the payroll cost was $66 million and that the federal government had agreed to pay $33 million, half the payroll cost. The total federal contribution under a program costing $200 million was the figure mentioned by the minister, half the labour cost or $33 million.
As good as this winter works program is, so far as it goes, it does not really represent on the part of the government a vigorous confrontation of this problem. To the extent that the program is effective the credit should not go to the Minister of Labour or to this government but to the combined endeavours of the provinces and municipalities.
When we last discussed this matter the Minister of Labour said the average labour content of all municipal works was 34.5 per cent, and since the federal government paid only 50 per cent of the direct labour cost the federal share of the cost of such projects last year amounted to only 17 per cent. The conclusion to be drawn, as I have said, is that the municipalities involved bear the major brunt of the expenses incurred under the program.
The minister just reminded us that seven provinces were paying an additional 25 per cent of the payroll costs; that Quebec was paying 40 per cent, and that Manitoba had increased its contribution to 50 per cent with respect to employment provided for persons who had been on social assistance for a continuous period of 90 days. The minister did not, however, announce any substantial improvement in the contribution of the federal government to the operation of the winter works program.
I have already indicated that seasonal swings in unemployment have their greatest impact in distressed areas such as the maritime provinces. Because of this, the distressed

communities are the ones least capable of covering the two thirds of the total cost which must be met by the municipalities. That is why we in the Liberal party suggested the establishment of a municipal loan fund which would greatly aid the affected communities in contributing their share of the cost of the projects.
The fact is that more men and women could be put to work under this program if the government either bore a greater share of the burden of the cost of the program or was willing to establish a municipal loan fund which would enable the municipalities to obtain the necessary revenues to carry out certain projects which they are not carrying out under this program now, because of the terms of financing as among the three levels of government, and because, in so many instances the municipalities cannot possibly bear the burden involved.
Lest there be any doubt of this let me make reference to the figures I have before me. I have in my hand figures relating to the winter works program in Toronto, the largest city in Ontario. I find that in the year 1960-61 the city's share of the cost of that program was 61.3 per cent. I ask hon. members to reflect on this. The city of Toronto has had to meet the problem of unemployment to the extent of 61.3 per cent in respect of a program the responsibility of which is shared three ways but mostly, in this case, by the city of Toronto, second by the province of Ontario, and to a much lesser extent by the federal government.
The federal government wishes to accept all the credit for this program. By its advertising and by the implications of the do it now campaign the impression is given that this government which said it was going to see that no one suffered from unemployment is solely responsible for whatever is being accomplished under this wholly inadequate program, one that is not sufficiently vigorous to meet the problem as it should be met.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question at this point? Would the hon. gentleman refer to his notes and put on record the extent to which the 61 per cent, the city's share, of the cost of that program is represented by building materials and the extent to which the 61 per cent represents direct payroll costs?
I do not have those figures.
Oh, oh.

If my hon. friend has them I have no doubt that they reveal that this represents a very considerable purchase. But I am not thinking of the assistance
Supply-Labour
given to those who sell such materials. I am thinking of whether or not this program as a whole is designed to provide employment to a greater number of men and women than have been put to work or affected by it to date.
That is the problem to which the mayors of Canada address themselves every time they consider this question in relation to the winter works program. The mayors of Canada met the government on November 10 last. While they were grateful for the combined consequences of this program through the three levels of government, they certainly were not satisfied with what had been achieved to date.
In their brief they point out that one of the major obstacles to fuller municipal participation is lack of any provision for financial assistance toward the cost of materials. This is an old demand of the municipalities, repeated again. They say another obstacle is the very real difficulty some municipalities have in obtaining the money needed for capital undertakings, and at reasonable interest rates. That confirms the desirability of the concept and program of the municipal loan fund which the Liberal party has recently put forward. They point out that still another difficulty is that it is not practicable for municipalities, although they are willing to reschedule their work requirements as much as possible to the winter season, to make a sharp division between seasons.
They make certain other proposals which the government to date has given no indication of considering. They propose that federal loans be provided to municipalities for capital work projects at a favourable rate of interest, extending the practice now followed in the financing of sewage facilities. Second, they propose that federal contributions to municipal works be extended throughout the year with the federal government contributing a proportionately greater share of the cost of material involved in such work undertaken during the winter months of the year. If this is not feasible, they urge that the time be extended to permit completion of projects already commenced during the winter season.
Their third proposal is that municipal works for which federal aid is available under other forms of assistance be considered as allowable projects for federally assisted municipal winter works program. I presume that railway grade crossings would be an example under that proposal. The next proposal is that measures be taken to assure prompt interim payment of the federal government's share and early final settlement of all federally assisted municipal programs.
It is clear that there should be an extension of the types of projects now coming under

Supply-Labour
the winter works program. I am sure that the proposals to which I have just referred are not the only suggestions that should be considered. In order that the winter works incentive program may have its major impact upon the communities that need it most, I suggest that federal participation should be on a sliding scale depending on the amount of unemployment in a particular area. At present the program is not having a major impact on the communities that need it most. If my suggestion is not adopted the situation will continue under which the communities that are not in dire need of this type of assistance will postpone work which would normally be done in the summertime, as they are now doing, in order to take advantage of the government's partial coverage of the labour costs incurred during the winter. As a consequence, certain areas with less than the national average of unemployment are receiving a proportionately greater share of the additional employment created by the program.
I ask the Minister of Labour if it is not a fact that some of the areas where unemployment levels are highest are the areas that are least able to take advantage of the assistance under this program. The names of some of the cities in this category were put on Hansard last year and they could be repeated. Right in Ontario areas like Cornwall, Windsor, Oshawa, Peterborough-
We are not a distressed area now.

I am not talking of distressed areas. I am talking about areas where there is unemployment and there is great unemployment in Peterborough. These communities do not have as many projects as other communities in Canada where the problem is less severe. If the government was really on its toes, if it really had an unemployment program it would be one that would be addressed particularly to those areas where unemployment is heaviest.
But all that the government does is to go through a demonstration of apparent activity without rationalizing its program or making it applicable in those areas where it would do the most effective job. Why does the government not expand this program if it really wants to bite into the problem of unemployment? Why should it not pay for a portion of the materials used? That, it has been demonstrated by the mayors, would be one way to reach many more unemployed in this country. Why does it not act upon the suggestion that the federal government should pay a substantial portion of the
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
supervision costs? This would assist two municipalities in Ontario that I know of in taking greater advantage of this program.
Why does the federal government not give some consideration to the reduction or elimination of the sales tax on building materials used on projects designed to give work during the winter period? If it really wants to meet this problem of unemployment, why does it not act on the proposal that this might be done as it is being done in the United States, by tax incentives such as increased depreciation allowances based on wintertime construction payrolls applied to industrial and commercial projects?
The minister spoke a while ago of the approval given to this program by the Canadian Construction Association. This association has recommended some of these very things but the minister gives the impression that these organizations that have spoken of the positive aspects of the program are completely satisfied, when such is not the case. Why should the federal government not bear a more substantial share of the cost of construction machinery used on a project such as bulldozers, trench diggers for sewers and the like? If the government really wants to make its contribution more effective, if it really wants to justify the designation which its propaganda machine has sought to achieve for this federal program, why does it not embark upon some of these proposals?
This matter continues to be a serious one in our country, Mr. Chairman. We would have thought that the government in this session prior to an election would have displayed toward this question the fever, agitation and concern that it has in certain other aspects of government activity represented by the program that it has announced in the speech from the throne. This government will be held to account when the next federal election comes, just as it has been held to account in this house for not having embarked upon policies in keeping with its assurance that no one would suffer in this country for want of work. The government has failed to live up to this promise notwithstanding the statement of the Prime Minister that practically all of his promises have been fulfilled. This is one promise that has not been met and no amount of adulation of the government's anaemic program is going to change this picture when, as of the month of December last, 413,000 people were out of work, more proportionately than in any other country in the western world. I ask the minister to tell me what the unemployment figures are in Great Britain, what they are in Germany, what they are in Switzerland, what they are in Belgium-
Japan?
-what they are in the Scandinavian countries.
What are they in the United States?
What are they in the United States? I say that in the United States the problem is severe but it is not as bad as it is here.
That is not so. Look at the record.

One reason why the situation is not as bad there is that they have in charge of their affairs an imaginative head of government who is trying to fulfil the promises he made to the electorate of that country. This has not happened here.
Are you speaking of the speech the president made the other day or of legislation which has been enacted by congress? My hon. friend knows there is a great difference.

I am speaking of the leadership given in the United States with regard to this problem by the President since he became the President of the United States. I am referring to the state of the union message last year and this year and the way congress has acted upon his recommendations, their program of accelerated depreciation, their examination of the problem in distressed areas and so on. No legislative body in the United States has been refused the opportunity to examine into the unemployment situation. When I think of the fact that during the last four and a half years the present government has denied the House of Commons the right to examine the problem of unemployment in a committee, I say that in the face of that fact alone the government has demonstrated that it has not confronted the problem of unemployment in the manner in which it assured the Canadian people it would.
May I ask the hon. member a question? What is the proportion of unemployment in the United States?

The other place examined this problem. Members of the other place made a valuable study, a study that should have been made by the Department of Labour, a study that might well have been made by this house where the elected representatives of the people could have called before the committee all kinds of witnesses to ascertain the nature of the problem. In the town of Moncton, for instance, there is a great deal of unemployment. We should have had a parliamentary committee and should have been able to call the heads of the railroads
Supply-Labour
before that committee to find out why their program in that particular community did not allow for the continuation for a particular level of unemployment. It would have been valuable to find out why and offer a solution.
We should have had a parliamentary committee so that we could have called representatives of the automobile industry before it and have found out why unemployment was taking place at particular levels, what was the percentage of automation and what the possibility was of rectifying the problem. We could have gone into the same matter with regard to the town of Peterborough. We could have examined why in the city of Cornwall last year 14,000 people were out of work.
The House of Commons was denied that opportunity because the government was apparently unwilling to allow any committee of this house to examine into the causes of unemployment and propose remedies for the simple reason that the government was not prepared to embark on policies which a committee of that sort would be likely to recommend. That is the situation.
It is all very well for the government to say that there are more men in the work force now. Of course there are more men in the work force. The population is larger. Our birth rate is continuing its normal course. Of course there are more men in the work force. But what does that prove? That does not in any way deal with the problem of unemployment. In the face of the promises made by this government, in the face of the fact that we now have over a quarter of a million men and women out of work, this government cannot hope to escape the indictment that as a government it has not faced up to its responsibilities.
