Mr. Chairman, once again we are called upon to pass an estimate in order to provide this government with its answer to unemployment, the winter works incentive program. The minister ended his remarks by saying it was a worth-while program, that it was a successful program and because of the excellence of this program there would be no difficulty in securing the passage of this item-this in spite of the fact, as the hon. member for Essex East said, there may be
413,000	people unemployed in our nation and probably even more than that at this very moment.

Supply-Labour
I took the time to look over the remarks made by the minister on this item in other years. According to him this program was a success in 1958-59 when 41,000 men received work. The minister has a penchant for large figures. He assumes that five weeks of work for an individual provides him with work for the winter. According to the minister, in Canada we have five weeks of winter.
It was nine weeks work.

Then, surely, we should suggest not 41,000 but 20,000 for 1958-59; 25,000 for 1959-60 and 60,000 for 1960-61. We should be able to place some reliance upon the statistics that are given in connection with this matter of winter works. The program was a success last year when, as we have heard, we had more unemployment in Canada than there was in any other country in the western world and when we failed completely to deal with the program which faced us. If we include those who are dependant upon those who are unemployed, then probably 1.5 million people in this nation are suffering. Unemployment has blighted the hopes of many young people so far as future education is concerned because their parents have no hope of a stable income.
We are told that this program is a success, a worth-while project. Why are we told this? We are told this because the government does not know what success means. There are no goals. They refuse to set goals. They refuse to organize or direct the economy in order to achieve goals. Anything which provides employment is therefore a success. There is no measure of success; there is no measure of failure. All they have to do is add up the figures and tell us there were so many more people in the work force, so many more employed. This becomes therefore success with a capital "S".
Over the last number of months, and over the last number of weeks particularly, there has been considerable glee and rightly so. I am sure all of us are extremely happy to find that the percentage of unemployed has been going down. This does not result from anything this government has done. They have no reason to take any credit for this fact. After all, it was only last winter that this government said you could not do anything about unemployment. When the unemployed marched on Ottawa, the Prime Minister said this was a free enterprise society; this government could do nothing for them. Every few weeks the Minister of Trade and Commerce came forward with a solution. It was his theme song; management and labour must sit down together. Yes, this is like being in favour of motherhood. Indeed,

labour and management must sit down together, but who is going to provide the opportunity? Who is going to set the rules? Who is going to give some kind of assurance that when management and labour do sit down together and come to a conclusion there will be someone who is going to provide some direction, some kind of purpose to the economy so that both will have the assurance that neither will be at a disadvantage because they have sat down together.
When this government does get management and labour to sit down together and a report is made to the government, then the government forgets completely what they have said. There is no follow-up. How strange it is that this government is actually now taking credit for lowering the number of unemployed in our society. This action is strange indeed on the part of a government which has refused to plan, refused to give any direction and is only tinkering about and hoping that they do not drop a wrench and completely destroy the machinery.
Well, because of activities in other sectors, notably in the world trade movement, because of the strengthening of the economy of our neighbours to the south, there are fewer unemployed. The minister, therefore, brings before us smother winter works incentive program and tries to convince us that this is the kind of dynamic leadership which we should expect from a Conservative government, I could not help but find rather amusing article in the Globe and Mail of October 3. Our Prime Minister was then down in Dunnville speaking to the Haldimand county Progressive Conservative association, and according to this article he remarked upon the fact that the percentage rate of unemployment was going down. Canada had a rate of only 4.8 per cent, said the Prime Minister, and this is not abnormally high when economists regard 3 per cent to 4 per cent as the flexible part of the labour force. Even when we cannot reach minimal levels it is apparently all right.
On the same page in the Globe and Mail we have another article which states that direct relief costs jumped 40.6 per cent. The unemployment insurance offices are not so crowded today nor are the national employment offices because all the unemployed are over in the municipal welfare offices. In my own municipality in the month of September welfare rolls doubled as compared with the past year. We regard with some eagerness the fact there are so few people on unemployment insurance, but the truth is many of these people are dependant entirely upon municipal relief.
What is wrong with this program is the fact, of course, that it is completely and

utterly inadequate for the kind of unemployment that Canada is facing and will face. The program just tries to deal with seasonal unemployment. The minister knows very well that this is only one small aspect of the whole unemployment picture of this nation. Indeed, it is one of the lesser aspects of the unemployment problem in the last few years. In the middle of summer last year we were over what could be called a full employment society. But what about technological unemployment? What are we going to do about that? What about cyclical unemployment? We all know that the economy has started to run now; it has started to move slowly. What will happen by 1966? We will be in the same mess again. Now is the time, if ever Canada had the opportunity to take hold of this problem and deal with it. We should deal with it now when we are not so overwhelmed with this tremendous problem of mass unemployment. Now, when the unemployed are starting to move back into employment, we can decide that never again will Canada have to face mass unemployment with 800,000 or 900,000 unemployed people in our nation.
This is the challenge, and what do we get? We get another winter works program. That is all this government can do, just look about three or four months ahead. If they survive that long, then evidently that is success. This is a worth-while project and one which will not need to be defended on the floor of this house. That is the first thing that is wrong with this program. It is completely inadequate to cope with the various complexities of unemployment with which we are going to be faced over the next decade.
Second, of course, and this has already been touched upon by the hon. member for Essex East, this program does not help those who most need help. The federal government pays only one half of the labour cost. As we have seen, this is only a fraction of the total cost, perhaps only one dollar or two dollars out of the ten dollars which the municipality will pay towards these works. I should like to see a breakdown of these projects. I should like to see a number of winter works projects carried out in Amherst and New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, in the province of Quebec, in Lindsay, Ontario, and other areas which this government decided were areas of surplus manpower and required to be given particular attention.
And Hamilton.

In that particular sphere we spent a long enough time trying to find out which areas would be selected. We spent from December to March trying to find out what plan was going to be implemented, and it was months later before any of these areas were
Supply-Labour
designated. Indeed, we can remember being told that once they were designated we would see the opening of the gates of paradise, and that there would be industries scrambling to get into these areas.
How many industries have been brought into the surplus manpower areas?
A total of one.

According to the minister there have been nine-only nine new industries all across the whole of the dominion. He says that these works cut unemployment, but all I can find is that a large number of workers still have to find jobs in surplus manpower areas. This program is the kind of niggling and tinkering which has been going on, and which will completely destroy us should we try to compete with other nations that have decided to do something about the problem of unemployment.
Only last month I was amused to read an article from a publication in Sydney, Australia. It is headed: "Unemployment the key issue in Australian election." My first reaction was that I was going to learn a lot about great unemployment in Australia, and once in a while it is comforting to learn that other countries share the same problem that we have. One feels we are completely out of step when we read of West Germany inviting
70,000	workers into that country, and reading that they have stopped unemployment insurance because of over contribution to the unemployment fund in that country. In Sweden they are absolutely shocked at the level of unemployment here in Canada. Indeed, it has been said that our Department of Immigration might well be called the department of emigration as more people are trying to get out of the country. For these reasons I thought there would be some comfort for me in the article on unemployment in Australia. There was none. It reads:
There is no denying that unemployment is worrying many Australians. Official government figures place the total unemployed at 96,552 representing 2.3 per cent of an estimated 4,200,000 work force.
Only 2.3 per cent of the labour force in Australia is unemployed, yet last winter we had 10 per cent, 11 per cent, 12 per cent, and in some parts of the country 15 and 18 per cent of our labour force unemployed. It is no wonder I say it was amusing to read that article which said unemployment was a major election issue in Australia.
How far out of step can this country get? I should like to know how much money is really being spent in these areas which need it so desperately. In spite of all the drawbacks of what little they are getting, we would certainly hope for better progress in those areas where it is so desperately needed.

Supply-Labour
My third point of criticism about the program is that the projects are entirely short term ones. They do not really give any hope of employment. At the most they give five weeks employment-five weeks when the men working do not have to turn to some other source of income.
Last November and December I took the opportunity of going through the nearby armoury to see what was going on in the government's survival program. There were some 2Q0 people talking part in it over there. Whether we agree with survival or not, at least they were looking after their own survival and getting paid by the government of Canada. Who were these people?
The unemployed.

That is right. The hon. member for Essex East says they were the unemployed. They were the people I had seen standing in front of the unemployment insurance office and the welfare office, but when they approached the government last winter the government told them: "We cannot give work. This would be undermining our free enterprise system." Has it come to this that the only way we can use our imagination is by putting men in uniform? Is that the only way we can provide a decent wage for at least a few weeks? Is it not a disgrace that a person would have to say that about a country which has all the opportunities of this nation?
There are no long term projects under the winter works incentive program. Instead of such projects we have a whole group of small -not insignificant but extremely limited- types of projects. Only a year ago my own city tried to get a grant for industrial site clearance work. It was a very sensible plan for a municipality with a large number of unemployed to prepare an area for the incoming industries that might be provided, that might be interested in moving there, but it was not accepted as a winter works program project. In passing I might say I am glad that the program is being widened now, but not sufficiently in my view. This government does not believe in public works. The Minister of Public Works himself has said that. According to him "you cannot expect public works to provide real employment." Can anyone imagine a more completely directionless cabinet where we have one minister standing up telling us how much has been done to provide employment, and another minister standing up and saying they cannot really provide employment? This is another example of the dichotomy of thinking in this particular field.

My fourth criticism, and most serious charge against the winter works program, is that it misleads the people of this nation into believing that this is all that a federal government can do, that this is the sum total of the federal government's duty to deal with the national problem of unemployment.
A few minutes ago I said that in 1962 we would be in a position to do something dynamic about our economy, that we would be coming out of the doldrum, but will we then have had the same kind of directionless, ridiculous growth, unproductive growth at least in terms of national growth and employment. I said that we should have a disciplined, sensible, planned growth in place of municipal works programs. That, I believe, is the only thing that can provide the kind of full employment this nation must have.
I think I heard an hon. member say that we cannot provide full employment. That is an interesting remark to make in terms of what the rest of the world is doing. A winter works program is not the alternative. How can this nation compete on such a basis with the nations of the European common market? How can we compete with Britain and other countries in the commonwealth? How can we compete with the possibility of competition from the communist world when we have 300,000, 400,000 and 500,000 unemployed?
Can we afford to pay for this unemployment? Industry pays for it in unemployment insurance benefits and also pays for it in property taxes. In other words, we have got this expense on our backs while we are trying to compete with other countries in this very competitive world. There is no alternative to full employment. This is not some kind of luxury which we can afford in the twentieth century. Those of us who believe it is are living in a fairy land.
It is fine to set up productivity councils, but how can we get labour and management to sit down together in a productivity council if what they are doing in effect is producing less jobs? The labour force has learned from the plight of the agricultural workers over the last 15 years. They have "produced" themselves down to the point where there are only half as many of them as there were 10 years ago. The agricultural worker has improved his production to the extent that he only gets half of the material rewards for his work that he should get. Instead of 12 per cent of the national income he gets 6 per cent. Unless this government can find something more than a winter works program it is utterly futile to try to suggest that productivity councils have the answers to the economic problems of the nation.
I think we were all somewhat discouraged by the howling that went on over in Europe

regarding Great Britain's entry into the European common market. What we fear most is that we cannot compete, with the kind of blundering, purposeless, directionless economy that we have. We are doing a little bit at a time; we are putting a little bit of oil in there with the municipal winter works incentive program.
This is what we should be doing, instead of a little bit of municipal building or reconstruction of parks. We know we are going to have a health plan. Two parties in this house have already said that they are in favour of it and the other party is now looking at the possibility of a royal commission providing the answer.
What will happen when we have a health plan? We will have a run on our hospitals such as we have never seen before, but we will not have the hospitals. What did we do last year? We spent millions and millions of dollars on unemployment insurance while men were standing with their hands at their sides when these hospitals could have been built.
We have set up a sports council and given them $5 million. We hope they will be able to develop some physical fitness in this nation. What are the problems this council will face? They will face a lack of facilities in this nation with its varied climatic conditions. What could we have been doing last year with the millions of dollars we were pouring into unemployment insurance and welfare, with all the money we were losing from taxation? We could have been building recreation centres across this nation into which this new sports council could have fitted this new program which has been spoken of so promisingly during the last few weeks.
This program is simply not enough. Toronto has already been mentioned. Out of a total of
67,000	unemployed in Toronto the winter works incentive program provided work for only 2,000. Two thousand out of 67,000. There is no long term plan; there is no planned development. Of course, the party in office has no interest in planning, no concern over planning and no real faith in planning.
We will vote for this measure. We will see this go through; but it will be with a heavy heart, realizing that there will still be hundreds of thousands of unemployed people in this country, some of whom have been unemployed for, not months but years.
We know that when we pass this measure they will still be unemployed; that countries in the world will still look at Canada and wonder why it is that this nation of all nations, with its tremendous resources, with all its opportunities, cannot solve a problem like unemployment. I am sure these countries will 26207-1-274
Supply-Labour
not hear very much about the municipal winter works program. I am sure they will not see headlines about this program in the Financial Post or in the newspapers which circulate in other countries of the world. They will look at us and wonder just what is wrong, if this is the best we can do.
We will watch this go through. We will know it will not be enough. We will know it will provide heartbreak for hundreds of thousands of people in this nation. If this is the measure of activity this government is prepared to take in dealing with this No. 1 national problem, we have little fear about what the electorate will do when the time of accounting comes at the polls.

Mr. Chairman, there is not very much I can add to what has been said by the two previous speakers. I think they have covered this subject quite thoroughly. However, there are a few things with which I should like to deal, and possibly underline one or two of the matters they raised.
The minister opened his statement on these estimates with a talk about the effectiveness of the great advertising we have seen on the do it now program. It reminded me of one evening a month or so ago when I was sitting with some people in my constituency and one of the favourite propaganda t.v. shots for this do it now program came on the screen. One of the people with whom I was sitting remarked that the thing he liked best in that particular commercial was where the carpenter sawed a hole and dropped the announcer down through the floor into the basement. He said, "That is the treatment that should be given to anyone who broadcasts that kind of poppycock". I will not go so far as to agree wholeheartedly with him. Possibly some good comes from that program, but I would be rather hesitant to estimate just how much.
The minister said something else that disturbed me. He seemed to think that with this increased activity in the winter works program we were going to balance off the employment picture in this country. In other words, many of the jobs that were previously carried out in the summertime would now and in the future be carried out in the wintertime because of this program.
I should like to remind the minister that this would not be a very favourable solution to the problems of this country. If under this government we are going to have from
700,000	to 800,000 unemployed in the wintertime, and from 300,000 to 400,000 unemployed in the summertime, all we will do by shifting the summer work to the winter will be to average it out so that we would have 550,000

Supply-Labour unemployed the year round. I certainly do not think this is any solution of which any government should be proud.
The minister also mentioned the past year's figure of $250 million which had been spent on this program. I was rather surprised at the hon. member for Essex East in this connection. I know he has been accused by government members of having a mathematical formula all his own, but I beg to differ with the conclusions at which the hon. member arrived. The minister said that some $250 million have been spent on this program and the federal government contributed $33 million. That works out at about 13.2 per cent. Then of course the government of Ontario contributes 25 per cent of the labour costs, which comes to 6.6 per cent, or a total from the two governments of 19.8 per cent. I think that to properly assess this program we must realize the position which faces the municipalities. First of all they must raise all the money that is to be spent on any of these projects. Then after they have raised it and proceeded with the project they can hope to be reimbursed 13.2 per cent of the cost from the federal government and 6.6 per cent from the provincial government. This still leaves the municipalities having to provide over 80 per cent of the cost of the project from municipal funds.
I have spoken on this item in previous sessions. I admit that the situation has been improved since this program was first started. There have been some changes and progress has been made in this regard. However, the fact remains that the programs subject to approval under this plan are very carefully selected programs. To qualify under this plan it appears that municipalities must have projects that could be more adequately handled by machinery than by manpower in this modem day and age. Of course, as we all know, neither the federal government nor the provincial governments make any contribution toward the cost of machinery or material, so it would seem that the projects which would be approved under this program are of such a nature-almost, one might say, from careful choice-that they cannot be too successful.
I do not wish to cover the field which has been covered by the two previous speakers, but I should like once more to underline some of the objections we have to this program and some of the shortcomings we find in it. I have brought these to the attention of the committee on previous occasions and the reason I am doing so again is because no attempt has apparently been made to remedy those shortcomings. This is called a winter

works program and in my opinion that is something of a misnomer. First of all, if we had winter work we should not need this program. In the second place, it will not work in winter; it only works in those parts of Canada where winter conditions are not too severe. In proof of this contention I point to the fact that this is the second year in succession in which, to my knowledge at least, there has not been one single project either in my own riding or in the riding to the north of it under this program. The reason is simple. None of the projects that can be approved under this plan can be carried out with any degree of common sense during the winters we have in the north country.
Another problem we have with regard to this winter works program is that it puts the municipalities in a most unfair position. At the time they strike their budgets they have no assurance that this plan will be in effect the following winter. Then, by the time the announcement comes along, their budgets have been struck and have gone before the municipal board for approval. Consequently, they have no provision made for participation in the program. I feel also, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Peterborough, that there is a great danger that this program is coming to be regarded as a solution to the unemployment problem. I think there is a very great danger in this approach. The unemployment problem is a direct problem and this particular scheme is a very indirect and very expensive way of meeting the problem.
It seems to me that the government should take a look around the world today. The people now responsible for the administration should look at what is being done in Sweden, West Germany, Denmark, Israel and other European countries which have full employment. Surely if this government has not the intelligence and the brains to do at least as well as the governments of those countries, then in heaven's name it is time they admitted it to the public and went back to the public for a decision.

It is a privilege to say a few words at this time and to congratulate publicly the minister and the federal cabinet upon having had the wisdom to bring forward this additional assistance in the amount of $40 million.
As the previous speaker, the hon. member for Timmins, has said, perhaps the name is a misnomer; it should generally be referred to as the federal-municipal winter works incentive program. My own remarks will be primarily confined to a few situations occurring in the province of New Brunswick. Last May I placed a question on the order

paper and as a result it became publicly-known that five provinces in Canada were contributing 25 per cent toward direct payroll costs to assist municipalities taking part in this program. The provinces of Quebec and Manitoba provided assistance in excess of that amount.
So far, the province of New Brunswick has not seen fit to extend financial assistance to municipalities in any way in order that the towns and cities in the province may take more advantage of the federal assistance. I strongly doubt whether much of this $40 million will be available to the towns and cities of New Brunswick and I say this because I do not feel the provincial administration is taking enough interest in the plight of unemployed people in the incorporated cities and towns.
Early in October the federal Department of Labour made public the number of projects accepted in New Brunswick up to October 16. I have a list in front of me, and 42 projects are listed. Only four of them would normally qualify as municipal projects but because of a generous amendment to the regulations which was primarily directed to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, highway works in those two provinces now qualify for assistance. Of the 42 projects in New Brunswick as of October 16, 1961, 38 dealt with the construction of bridges, seawalls along highways and work of a similar nature. Consequently, in an indirect manner, the province of New Brunswick is contributing to the payroll costs because it has placed itself, by interpretation, in the position of being a municipality.
I have no complaint to make about the province of New Brunswick taking advantage of federal assistance to rebuild bridges, seawalls and highways. However, I do feel, when I look at the figures and see that out of the first 42 projects only four were undertaken by municipalities, that somebody somewhere is not co-operating with Ottawa.
In addition, I believe that politics or provincial patronage are entering into the scheme. To explain what I have in mind, may I say this: the details outlined by the Minister of Labour to the premiers indicated that the national employment services throughout the country would be used in connection with placements for work provided by the program. If a program originates in a municipality, whether a city, a town, or a rural municipality, it becomes a public project which is submitted first to the provincial capital and then to Ottawa. The people who are unemployed, together with employees in the national employment service local offices
Supply-Labour
know all about the project. However, if the project is a provincial one in its entirety, one that is designed by the provincial government in camera, no one knows about it until Ottawa has given its approval. In the intervening days or weeks, friends, organizers and supporters of the provincial government tell local people that, for example, a bridge in their rural area is to be rebuilt. The same people are advised to apply to the local employment service office if they want work. Those who are supporters of the administration get this advance notice. They are immediately put on the list and referred to the provincial government garage concerned. Therefore, under this program one must, in my opinion, be a supporter of the Liberal administration of New Brunswick in order to get employment on a provincial project. I strongly criticize that practice. This is supposed to be a joint venture. The programs are under the partial administration of the federal government, but in most projects as stated earlier the provincial administration has complete charge.
I also want to point out to the minister that his written instructions of July 25 have not been entirely fulfilled. The letter to the premiers concluded by indicating that this was a federal-provincial-municipal program and that programs are to be advertised with signs making reference to the joint participation. I have yet to see a program in New Brunswick sponsored by the provincial government that in any way gives credit to the federal Department of Labour.
Turning to the subject of education the New Brunswick department of education and the provincial department of labour have brought out a program entitled "Basic Education Training Course" which has been extensively advertised on radio and television throughout the province. The advertisements are designed to attract people to enrol in order that they may improve their skills. These advertisements in no way give credit to the federal government notwithstanding the fact that 75 per cent of the costs of advertising, administration, teachers' salaries and other costs are contributed to the province by the federal government. The same situation may obtain in other provinces across the country. I suggest to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that where necessary, employees of the federal Department of Labour should have something to say in the preparation of television, radio and newspaper advertisements where the federal government contributes 75 per cent of the advertising expenditure. If a province will not co-operate, I further

Supply-Labour
suggest that employees oi the federal departments should be directed to take a personal interest in the matter at the local level to ensure that some of the bouquets and some of the credit are directed to the proper source.
Those are my basic criticisms. I am pleased to observe the wisdom, effort and interest the federal government is showing in the municipal winter works incentive program. However, I take issue with the fact that the program is not being administered in a fair way in my province.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of dwelling at length on this item, because I had the opportunity in the past of paying particular attention to this program which has been applied for the last four years.
I realize that, during the last three years the government has widened its scope, that is it allowed a larger number of projects; but I think the more important point is that in the four years since this government introduced this program it has failed to realize exactly what should be done.
I believe that I am not the only one to think so, because several hon. members who rose before me mentioned that, after all, this winter works program is not a federal program but a program financed by the provinces and, more particularly, by the municipalities. Nobody will, I think, deny what I just said, since it is also confirmed in the report published by the federal Department of Labour. Indeed, that report indicates that the contribution of the federal government for all those winter work projects comes down to only 15 per cent.
I may be accused of prejudice-
Which would be unfounded.

I should like, at this point, to read an editorial published in the Quebec newspaper Le Soldi of July 27, 1961, under the title "Municipal winter works-A poor way of solving the unemployment problem." I quote:

The article goes on to say:
That was something new, and a greater number of municipalities have developed large scale projects which are far from being all completed. We know something about it in Quebec-
And when reference is made to Quebec, it means Quebec city.
-where those projects had to be stopped following violent snowstorms.
Here is, in my opinion, the main point raised by the members of the opposition since the introduction of this winter works program. I quote:
Those works are still costing a lot of money, too much, to municipalities, which are shouldering crushing burdens and which are requesting more sources of income from higher levels of government.
Here, I should like to digress a little in order to remind the house that during the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958, this government had promised to give municipalities-not only the provinces-a share of the national income, in order that they could fulfil their constitutional responsibilities. Well, we know that nothing has come out in this regard. The article goes on to say:
The inadequacy of their current resources has obliged them to resort to massive loans. Issues of bonds are succeeding one another, and municipal debts are increasing at a rate which cannot last indefinitely. Several municipalities find it impossible to secure new loans. That is why they are requesting greater assistance, without obtaining any satisfaction.
I shall end the quotation here for the moment.
I say once again that, for the past three years, we have asked the government for a greater assistance instead of the mere 15 per cent granted now.
If, at the time of the 1957-1958 elections, municipalities and provinces had been told that they would have to find by themselves a solution to the unemployment problem, I am sure that many of our friends now sitting on the government side would not be here today.

REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL GRID
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the advisability of talcing the appropriate steps necessary for the early establishment of a national power grid which would be utilized to develop Canadian industry and provide employment opportunities through development of all natural power resources. And that the government should consider providing the necessary research and technical study and the calling at the earliest possible date of a dominion-provincial conference to implement the national power grid authority.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it would appear that this idea is not unique within myself. As you know, we introduced this resolution before we were aware of what was in the throne speech. Having heard the speech from the throne, we are now aware that the government and in particular the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) have decided to do something about the matter of a national power grid.
I believe all Canadians are aware of the need to solve the problem that is developing because of the fact that at the extreme ends of Canada there is a great potential of electrical power while in the central part, particularly in the province of Ontario, a shortage of power is rapidly developing. The extent of the shortage is indicated by the fact that in Ontario the arctic watershed and the rivers that flow northward in that area are now being developed for power purposes. This in itself is a strong indication that in Ontario we have about reached the end of our hydroelectric power development.
Saturday Night pointed out on January 6 of this year that installed potential horsepower in Ontario was 7,814,562 and of that amount 7,701,000 was being used. This would indicate that there is less than one million horsepower available in Ontario at the present time. It was recognized a long time ago that the economic problems in developing a country of this nature were going to be tremendous and that there were economic factors which naturally led to a north-south flow of trade. To overcome this situation, the first prime minister of this country promised the people that he would build and did build a railway system to counteract that natural flow and to create an economic flow across Canada from east to west and west to east. We believe that the railway has now to some extent served its purpose of making it possible for us to develop a Canadian economy.
We are now concerned about another very large natural resource with which we are going to have to do something and which again is creating problems similar to those involved in the natural north and south
Request for Establishment of Power Grid flow of trade in earlier days. This situation has been brought forcibly to the attention of the Canadian people because of the poor handling and mismanagement of the Columbia power development. The Canadian people are faced with the proposal of exporting power to the United States or doing something about supplying that power to Canadian markets. Electric power cannot be held or stored. You cannot put it in a tank and keep it; you have to use it. You also cannot keep the resource that produces the power. The water is going to go over the dam or down the river no matter whether there is an electric power plant there.
So it is essential that when we can develop hydroelectric power we should do so. The people of British Columbia are now in the position of wanting to increase the amount of power in that province and they are going to be faced with the situation of the federal government saying that there shall be no export of power, or no export on such a short term basis that it is not practical, and the provincial government saying that they are going to export that power on their own terms.
In the Globe and Mail of November 26, 1961 there is a report of a speech made by the Prime Minister in Newfoundland and it contains this passage:
A hint that a national power grid plan is in the works was dropped Saturday night by Prime Minister John Diefenbaker. He said it may not be too long before such a grid could be established using new techniques in long haul transmission of power.
I suggest that the Prime Minister was flying a kite to see what the reaction of the Canadian people would be to long transmission lines and the establishment of a national grid. Obviously the results must have been favourable. The matter must have been discussed a good deal between that time and the opening of parliament this year because the speech from the throne contained an indication that something was going to be done to develop a national power grid.
I think the Canadian people should be treated more fairly with regard to the matter of a national power grid. It is a very important step and if the Prime Minister were really serious about doing something he would know that research and development work is necessary to adapt the system that has been developed in other countries of using d.c. power transmitted in heavy concentration over long transmission lines. He should know that this system needs to be adapted to the Canadian scene and that this takes research and work. If he really believes that something should be done about this matter, then this a field that obviously is

Request for Establishment of Power Grid within federal jurisdiction and he does not need any support from the provinces to make a start on it.
Certainly the implication was left that the government wants to have a line as soon as possible that will take surplus power developed in one place in Canada and transmit it to another area that can use it, and if this is so I think the government must say that it will supply the power grid on a national basis to those provinces that want to join in the implementing of such a plan.
I am quite sure that other speakers will say that we have to take into consideration the British North America Act and the constitutional issues, but what consideration did we give to constitutional issues when we wanted to build a national highway? When we instituted the trans-Canada highway certain provinces did not agree to come into the plan and only recently have they participated in it. I think the government of the day was farsighted enough to realize that they had to take the responsibility of providing the vehicle for developing a Canadian highways system. They did so and the provinces that wished to co-operate did so under that scheme.
I believe this is not a constitutional issue. In my view the government is going to try to blame the province of Quebec and say, "It is not our fault there is not going to be a national power grid". The government will have read in the Gazette today, as everyone else has, the headline: "Power Grid Proposal Gets Answer. It is No."

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL GRID
speechtext:
As the hon. member should know, we on this side of the house have great difficulty in introducing resolutions that will avoid reference to the expenditure of money. The resolution must be couched in such terms that the government will be able to manoeuvre. The resolution must simply ask the government to take into consideration rather than referring to the spending of the money that would be necessary to build a grid.
In reading this article, Mr. Speaker, one finds that the premier of Quebec refers to the constitutional issue which I suggest will be the major factor in determining what will be done. However, there are much more important factors to be taken into consideration. The premier of Quebec says, in effect, "This
[Mr. Peters.1

is a field of provincial jurisdiction and I consider that is where we must let the matter rest."
Is it not a fact, Mr. Speaker, that about a year or so ago this house passed a measure to enable the federal government to participate in the establishment of a maritime power grid? It is true that this power grid could not be considered national in scope, but it did extend over several provinces in the mari-times. If we are so interested in protecting the export of power, and I agree we must protect the export of power from Canada, is it not the responsibility of the federal government to make certain at the earliest possible moment there is a substitute method for handling the surplus power that will be developed? If we established a transmission line, you can call it a national transmission line, a national power grid or whatever you want, I believe the Canadian people would want to see a large concentration of secondary industry in Canada in order to use our natural resources.
I have spoken to some of the people in British Columbia and they are not averse to exporting power to the other provinces of Canada if the need is there. What they wish is the right to sell their power and they are certainly willing to give preference to the Canadian market. I am quite sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) suggested this plan in all seriousness and that he has been advised as to the feasibility of it. I hope that the government will take a much stronger position in this field and, since there is apparently not going to be unanimous agreement amongst the provinces, establish a national power grid in those provinces that will take advantage of it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this will be a very lengthy and very expensive program. We will be moving millions of kilowatts of electricity across a national power grid. We will not necessarily have to transport this power great distances because our country is so broad the time zones will vary the peak load periods, so surplus power can be transmitted east to west or west to east. There is another factor that should be borne in mind. These transmission lines will be useful not only for the transmission of hydro power, which appears to be the cheapest method of producing electricity at the moment, but these lines will be available to transmit electricity developed by thermal power or by nuclear power. It will be possible for us, through watching developments in other countries, to transmit a large amount of power from those areas now producing it.
One of the problems I have encountered, and this is particularly true of my own area, is that we have continued to export natural

resources in the raw state. We have seen the end or close to the end of several of our natural resources without gaining any secondary industry to replace these primary industries. I am sure the same situation exists in the maritimes and in the prairies where many farmers are being displaced by automation. This plan seems to me to present an opportunity for the Canadian people to take advantage of the tremendous resources we now have. Resources can be built upon and increased as the need becomes evident. Secondary industries depend entirely on such things as low cost power and a ready access to markets. I would think, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian people would watch the development of this program very carefully.
It is a fact that a private member cannot introduce all the implications that should be introduced into a resolution of this nature. The government is in a position to do something about this, whereas a private member is not. We are in a position in Canada, I think, where we can offer those provinces willing to take advantage of this national grid, all the beneficial results that will flow from such a plan. I would suggest that although Quebec has turned down this plan, it will be one of the first to take advantage of a program of this type. I can foresee the tremendous potential of some developments in the near future such as the one at Hamilton falls in the Labrador area. This will be an interprovincial development that will bring power to the north shore of Quebec and I am sure some of the surplus would be available to Ontario and the maritime provinces if these transmission lines are established.
I suggest this government will be remiss in its duty if it tells the public, "If it were not for this terrible Liberal in Quebec, we would have a national power grid." I do not believe it is the responsibility of a single Liberal in Quebec to squash this plan. It is up to the Conservative government in Ottawa to take the bull by the horns and develop a national power grid. I believe the Canadian people will respond to this plan with the same eagerness that they responded to the development of the national railway. It is obvious that this plan could result in the establishment of secondary industries. It will provide a blanket of cheap electricity. There will be periods when there will be surplus electricity that could be used by industries.
I hope that members on the government side will indicate that they, too, are interested in the federal government going ahead immediately with the research and development of this national project. Then those provinces that see an advantage in it, as British Columbia obviously does, will be able to start a 26207-1-28
Request for Establishment of Power Grid transmission line to handle the export of power to other provinces. It has been pointed out that this plan will be almost as important to the development of Canada in the next 20 years as was the development of the trans-Canada railway. I believe, knowing the developments that took place as a result of that project, the Canadian government should give immediate consideration to the implementation of a project that will not require the co-operation of all provinces. We should begin immediately with the co-operation of those provinces that wish to join in the establishment of a national power grid.

I am very pleased to have this opportunity to speak to the motion introduced by the hon. member for Timiskaming. It was rather interesting to see how he got around the idea of "following John". The only way he could do it was to attack the sincerity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
As hon. members know, one paragraph inserted in the throne speech had to do with the establishment of a national power grid system. I think it should be put on the record, and I quote:
The provision of low cost electric power is one of the most important factors in the economic growth and industrial development of Canada. As a further step in the national development policy, my Prime Minister has invited the provincial governments to join with the federal government in early discussions of the steps that might be taken toward the establishment of long distance power transmission to link provinces and eventually the different regions of Canada.
I suggest, sir, that this attack on the sincerity of the Prime Minister by the hon. member for Timiskaming was not only uncalled for but was out of place. If he wishes to use his motion as a political attack then he is doing the country a disservice, he is doing himself a disservice, and is doing a disservice toward his constituents.

speechtext:
We have read the report in this morning's Gazette about the response from the province of Quebec. This response, I suggest, is a political one and is not the response of sensible people in that province. To say "no, we won't even discuss it with you," does not seem to be very reasonable. I would suggest to the premier of Quebec, and perhaps to some of the premiers of the other provinces, that the idea they should build, not power grids but political power grids within their provinces, as some of them would like to do, is not in the interests of Canada as a whole. If we as a nation are to progress, then some of the political grids in
422	HOUSE OF
Request for Establishment of Power Grid some of the other provinces will have to accept the fact that co-operation is the only method that can make confederation work.
I have quoted the paragraph in the speech from the throne which deals directly with the problem. In effect the government has said that it intends to establish negotiations and discussions immediately with regard to the long distance transmission of power, and I am sure all Canadians will respond to the suggestion. Equally I am sure that a negative approach from one province will not hinder or stop discussions on a national power grid. Certainly the concensus coming from the resources for tomorrow conference was that the federal government must show the way in the development of Canada's resources, and I feel one of the major first steps in showing the way must be discussions upon and implementation of long distance power transmission.
We in Alberta are keenly interested in this subject because we happen to be in the happy position of having an abundance of energy producing sources. We have our hydroelectric developments that are now taking place, and those that can take place in the future. In my own constituency one of the major hydroelectric developments now being undertaken is on the Brazeau river, in the eastern foothills of the Rocky mountains, and there are plans for other rivers, the Athabasca, the McLeod, and the Pembina. All of these rivers flow down through areas which have tremendous natural resources, areas which are just now coming into their own and the resources of which are being considered for the very first time.
United States Steel is now investigating coke coal immediately north of Hinton and Edson, and there has been a tremendous upsurge in the exploration for and production of natural gas and its by-products. Very soon we shall have one of the first large thermal plants with the Calgary power plant being converted from natural gas back to coal. All of these resources, coal, gas, hydroelectric and petroleum by-products are primary sources from which electric energy can be made.
I do not know if the hon. member has mentioned that hydroelectric power remains the cheapest form of power, but I am sure there will come a time in the not too distant future when thermal plants fired by coal, gas and petroleum by-products will take a strong position in the production of electric energy.
A power grid system does not have to be trans-Canada at the start. Indeed we could have regionalization in the west, connecting the prairie provinces and British Columbia with the primary market in the north and to the east. Certainly the need for power is just


now becoming apparent in the northern territories. With the development of our natural resources at Pine Point, beyond Yellowknife, and at the Great Slave lake the power requirements of that area will be tremendous and could be most easily served by a grid connecting Alberta, British Columbia and the northern territories. Other regional transmission grids could be constructed elsewhere particularly in the maritimes, including the one mentioned by the hon. member at Hamilton falls.
It is my belief we should look at the problem of the transmission of power in the same way as we looked at the problem of the transmission of other forms of energy. In this regard I refer to the trans-Canada pipe line relating to gas. These energy sources should first be offered to the Canadian people and then, when we are sure that our own requirements are satisfactorily met and our future assured, we can go on to consider the export of surplus energy.
In this connection I may mention our national oil policy which has worked so well. We suggested to the oil companies that they meet quotas for production in the various oil fields. We exported oil into the western United States and we imported it back in the eastern area, and some consideration should be given to such a plan in regard to the use of electric power.
I am sure that everyone in Canada will look forward with pleasure to the implementation of a national power grid under the dynamic leadership of the present Prime Minister. I believe the power grid will go ahead and, notwithstanding some resistance in certain parts of the country, will become a major plan in the development policy and growth of Canada. I believe it will be brought in by a Conservative government as was the original trans-Canada railway in 1867.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say a few words in connection with the motion of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) concerning the establishment of a national power grid in Canada.
Obviously, every one of us welcomes developments of some scope in this country, because they always have a deep impact on the expansion and the economy of Canada and, consequently, on the income of the Canadian people.
As the hon. member for Timiskaming said, it was not so long ago when visiting Newfoundland the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) left the people of that province with the idea that a national

Request for Establishment of Power Grid
power grid might be established. I suppose, as suggested by the hon. member, he wanted to know the views of some Canadians and to receive suggestions. I think that such a line of action was not quite in good taste because, even if people accuse us of playing petty politics, as the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) did just now, when speaking of the constitution, I want to say- and those who do not admit it have not read the British North America Act or, if they have read it, they did not understand it- that our natural resources come under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
This does not mean that the provinces may not join in the implementation of national projects, after having met, considered the projects, and come to some agreement respecting the rights of each party, with the national interest in mind.
It has been said that Quebec's answer was of a political nature. Now, all the Quebec government said, was that natural resources come under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and Mr. Lesage added, as reported in the Gazette of January 31:
(Text):
After noting that power transmission is on the agenda of this summer's interprovincial conference of premiers at Victoria, B.C., of which Mr. Lesage is chairman, the letter stated:
"As a matter of fact, I have already opened talks on this subject with the premiers of other provinces''.
(Translation):
That is not exactly what was said by hon. members who spoke before me. I do not think his reply can be interpreted as a definite refusal. The premier of Quebec merely states that natural resources come under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but I do not think that he completely closed the door to any future discussion if no obstacle is put in the way of the talks that will take place this summer between the premiers of the different provinces.
In my opinion, it is entirely normal that the premiers should want to discuss such an important question which affects the rights of the provinces and, at the same time, can have great repercussions on the economy and development of the country.
In other words, I strongly support the first proposal put forward by the hon. member for Timiskaming, concerning the field of research related to that great project; I believe it is a very valuable proposal. In fact, the government has everything it requires to put to work a staff which could further research in that field.
Besides, an authority on the subject has already made some studies on the matter. I refer to Mr. H. L. Briggs, of the national 26207-1-28i
energy board. I should like to quote what he has written on the subject, not that I agree with his views, because I cannot express an opinion on such a complex issue, but I should like to have my colleagues understand that such a thing cannot be decided overnight. That question involves complications and complexities, and I have confidence in Mr. Briggs' judgement, although I do not know if everything he says will come about. But it would still be worth while to undertake and further these studies in order to ascertain the soundness of Mr. Briggs' claims, since, as everyone knows, he is an authority on the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make just a few remarks on this resolution which has been placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I have listened to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) and as far as hon. members on the other side of the chamber are concerned, I think it can all be boiled down to the fact that they are disappointed that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has again stolen a march on them.
Reference was made a short time ago-I believe by the hon. member for Timiskaming-to the grid system which has been set up in the maritime provinces between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. This grid system is most important to that area of the country. There is in my constituency a thermal plant, which of course uses coal, in the town of Trenton in Nova Scotia.
Just as an example of what a grid, even between two provinces, can do was shown in

the summer of 1960 when the province of New Brunswick was suffering from a lack of water and therefore could not use its hydro plants. At that time the plant in my area was able to supply a considerable amount of power to the province of New Brunswick. A grid system means a great deal to the receiving end and also to the transmitting end.
I recall attending a ceremony in 1960 in the constituency of the hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Kennedy) when the switch was pulled on the grid system which had been set up and is now maintained in an area known as lower Onslow in the county of Colchester.
Hon. members may ask, "Why is it important to your area?" I would point out that there are three coal mines in my area, the MacBean mine in Thorburn, the Drummond mine in Westville and the Greenwood mine in Greenwood. The thermal plant which transmits this power consumes a great deal of the coal from the Greenwood and Drummond mines and some from the MacBean mine. In fact it has been a godsend to the latter two mines because the coal they have is not of the best quality but can be burned in a thermal plant.
To give hon. members some idea of what this means to an area I wish to quote a few figures. This project was brought about by the introduction of the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, which was introduced by this government in 1957 as another forward step. The following figures were given by the then minister of mines and technical surveys last year when I asked him a question in the house. To the end of 1961, the following amounts had been paid. Subventions, $2.12 million; on transmission lines, $4.22 million, and for the Trenton plant, in my area, $2.86 million. For the year 1961, the estimates showed subventions amounting to approximately $1.7 million, $6.3 million for the building of transmission lines and for the completion of the addition to the plant in my area, $363,000. This is just between two provinces. The introduction of a national grid would not only help my own area but it would also help Cape Breton island inasmuch as a thermal plant could be constructed there and power sent to other provinces.
The situation in the province of Quebec was dealt with by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) and I do not think I need go into that question. For coal mining areas, for those areas in particular which were indicated by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) and, as well, for those which can supply waterpower, I think this would represent a most forward looking step on the part of the present government. I am sure

After I have made a few remarks about this motion I am satisfied the house will know that this government has not only been giving a great deal of attention to research into power development in this country, but has been doing something about it.
As the house probably knows, power in Ontario is the responsibility of the HydroElectric Power Commission. In the years since the commission was appointed or originated it has accomplished a very good job in the province of Ontario, not only in peacetime but in wartime. It has kept up with the increasing demand for power. The growth of the demand for power over the last number of years has been rapid, and the economists tell us that it will gain momentum as the years go by. The larger the population grows the more power will be used in line with the mode of living we have at the present time. Some economists predict a more rapid rate of growth than others but I think we can be satisfied that the growth will be rapid. The estimated increase for the demand for power in the province of Ontario over the next 20 years is between 5 per cent and 6 per cent per year. This means that the province of Ontario in 20 years' time will be required to double the supply of power that is needed today. Water sources of power in Ontario are, as the previous speaker has mentioned, about at an end. There are small sources up in the northern part of the province which will eventually be tapped but it is uneconomic at the present time to transport the power over the distance which would be involved. If the demand for increased power in the next 20 years were supplied from thermal sources it would mean an added cost, in coal, of some $300 million. No doubt a large amount of this coal would come from the United States, though some, of course, would come from Canada. According to this estimate it would cost $300 million a year to supply that amount of thermal power.
A short while ago the atomic energy board of Canada along with the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario agreed to erect an atomic power plant in the county of Bruce. Why they chose Bruce, I am not too sure; it is not because of the geniality of the hon. member who represents that constituency,
I know that. I suppose it is because we have the facilities required by such an important undertaking. The atomic power plant which is under construction at the present time is being built at Douglas point on lake Huron. The unit which is now under construction is expected to be completed by late 1964 or early 1965. The unit will produce 200,000 kilowatts. It is planned that in 1963 a second unit will be built in along with the first unit. That second unit is expected to produce another 200,000 kilowatts. There is talk at the present time of joining a third unit to the other two. The facilities are there.
Reverting to this question of the demand for power in 20 years time, I might point out that if this extra power were supplied by atomic energy it would mean there would be $150 million worth of uranium used per year to supply this plant. Coupled with the $300 million that would be spent on coal, this comes to a considerable sum. Power from this plant, when the plant comes into operation, will go into the hydroelectric power commission grid. I am sure it will not only supply the future industrial needs of our locality in Bruce but will make a contribution to supplying the needs of the rest of Ontario.
At this time I feel a national grid is something to which we can look forward but many of these bridges will have to be crossed before it will be feasible. If our population continues to grow on the basis of predictions, I am satisfied that such a grid will become a reality some time in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I do not usually take part in debates on private members' bills. But when I heard the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) a while ago, I felt I should intervene. After studying the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I agree with my colleague from Lapointe that this measure would infringe upon the autonomy of the provinces.
Along with my colleague from Lapointe, I believe that the development of natural resources comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and that any action in this regard must be initiated by provincial authorities. The hon. member for Lapointe pointed out that the federal government's intervention is justified in such a field, with the required consent and co-operation of provincial authorities.
I should not want to quarrel with him to no purpose on this matter, but it seems to me that he is at variance with some members of his party who were once influential. 1 refer

Request for Establishment of Power Grid in particular to the former member for Stormont, the present member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), who, not so long ago, that is last October 16, stated that the federal Liberal party is of the opinion that the joint programs should be abandoned. I therefore wonder how the hon. member for Lapointe can reconcile such an attitude with his party's general policy.
Perhaps he would like to know my views on that subject? He knows full well what my stand is concerning any question related to provincial autonomy.
I have often said in the house that any measure introduced by the central government which infringes upon provincial jurisdiction should be abandoned. Of course, it is not always easy to drop long standing programs but we must uphold the principle that the federal government should give up any measure which is prejudicial to provincial sovereignty, as determined by the British North America Act.
That is why I feel the hon. member for Lapointe must be in an uneasy position in that respect. I noticed the precautions he used, first saying that he recognized the provinces' sovereignty and jurisdiction in matters involving the development of natural resources, but that, on the other hand, he saw the possibility for the central government's intervention in matters involving natural resources, as long as the previous discussions had taken place between provincial authorities and the central government. It seems to me that this caution comes from a perfect knowledge of the present attitude of the Quebec government which, while saying that joint projects should be done away with, as did the premier of the province in 1960, at the federal-provincial conference in Ottawa, throws itself wholeheartedly, so to speak, into joint projects. Thus, it would appear that the careful attitude shown by the member for Lapointe is dictated by political and electoral considerations. I hope that he will soon explain matters. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I can only repeat what I have said about the measure introduced by the member for Timis-kaming. I do not see how he can reconcile the well known and recognized theory that development of natural resources comes under provincial jurisdiction with the project he is submitting to the house today.
I am not saying anything new when I say that relations between provincial governments and the central government have now reached a turning point, a kind of crossroads, and that we will soon have to do some new thinking about all the problems of our confederation, the problem of the various fields


of jurisdiction attributed to the central government and to the various provincial governments.
That is why it seems to me that any new action aiming at joining all the provinces through joint plans must be analysed with very special care. In fact, those joint plans, all those subtle and often occult links should not limit provincial sovereignty.
As far as the province of Quebec is concerned, a province which has always been staunchly autonomist for the last 15 or 16 years, it is easy to say that it intends-and I think all Conservative members from the province of Quebec share the same intention -to prevent any action being taken that would encroach upon that provincial sovereignty and jeopardize the over-all powers and exclusive rights which have been imparted to the provinces by the constitution of this country.
